claims.text: A conventional Ni–Cr–Mo steel can be manipulated by heat treatment to exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition is caused by control of temper embrittlement within a narrow temperature window.
The conventionally cast and quenched Ni–Cr–Mo steel has a homogeneous microstructure before the tailored heat treatment.
Tempering at selected intermediate temperatures promotes grain-boundary segregation of embrittling species.
Subsequent exposure to higher temperatures dissolves the grain-boundary segregants.
The alloy is ductile in the proposed low-temperature regime.
The alloy becomes brittle within a narrow intermediate tempering-temperature window.
The alloy recovers ductility in the proposed high-temperature regime.
Localized grain-boundary segregation of impurity or alloying elements mediates the temporary brittleness.
Grain-boundary segregation at intermediate tempering temperatures severely reduces intergranular cohesion.
Reduced intergranular cohesion causes a severe loss of ductility.
Redissolution of embrittling species into the matrix at higher temperatures restores ductility.
Untreated or conventionally heat-treated samples are expected to remain generally ductile without a clearly resolved reentrant transition.
The proposed transition is expected to occur only in conventional alloys such as Ni–Cr–Mo steels and not in compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys.
Transition temperatures and embrittlement severity vary with alloy composition and processing history.
